content.text: A service lifetime isn't a performance setting: it decides how long an instance lives and who shares it. A singleton keeps every dependency it was built with, so a scoped

it receives is shared by every request until the app stops. Development catches the common cases at startup and production checks nothing, so follow one rule: a service never lives longer than its dependencies.
A pull request changes one line:
. The reasoning sounds fine. The class keeps no state of its own, it runs on every product page, and one instance is cheaper than one per request. The unit tests pass, because they build

. Production starts without complaint. A day later, two bug reports arrive: price changes made in the admin panel no longer show on product pages, and under load some requests fail with "A second operation was started on this context instance before a previous operation completed". Nobody touched the database code.
is a performance knob. Singleton saves allocations, transient costs a few, scoped sits in between, and any service can depend on any other because the container wires them up either way.

It's an easy belief to hold. The lifetime docs do talk about cost: a transient service "incurs per-request allocations". A class whose only field is an injected dependency really does look stateless. And in production the container accepts the registration silently, so nothing suggests that a rule was broken.
The hidden assumption is that a class is stateless when its own code holds no state. Its dependencies count too.

is full of state: a change tracker, the operation in progress, a connection. Microsoft's guidelines actually point the other way: use a singleton only for a service whose own state is expensive to create or meant to be shared, and avoid it for services with no state, which are cheap to create as transients.
A singleton is built once, with everything it asks for

The container creates a singleton the first time it's requested and returns that same instance for the rest of the app's life. Its constructor runs once, so each dependency is resolved once and stored in a field. Whatever lifetime that dependency was registered with, it now lives exactly as long as the singleton. That's a
: a longer-lived service holding a shorter-lived one captive.
The captive comes from the root scope, not from a request

You might expect the singleton to keep the first request's instance. It doesn't. A singleton is resolved from the root provider, so its scoped dependencies come from the root scope, which no request ever uses. In a test, a middleware stored each request's tenant in a scoped
on every request. The docs describe the result: a scoped service created in the root container is effectively promoted to a singleton, and it's disposed only when the app shuts down.

items.text: A lifetime decides who shares an instance and for how long; performance is a side effect.
A singleton's dependencies are resolved once, from the root scope, and live as long as it does, whatever their own lifetime.
